summary: Suggests a simple way of delivering alphanumeric and numeric one-way pages to radio paging terminals. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 1861.

eli5.summary: A simple way for a computer to send short messages to someone's pager. A newer version replaced it.

subtitle: A simple protocol for sending alphanumeric and numeric pages over the Internet to radio pagers.

tldr.problem: Delivering pages to radio pagers typically requires modems, phone lines, and complex protocols like TAP (Telocator Alphanumeric Protocol). Users want an easier, standardized way to send pages through the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: SNPP provides a simple client-server protocol based on commands and numeric response codes, with two levels: Level 1 handles basic PAGE, MESSAGE, SEND, and QUIT operations; Level 2 adds multi-line messages, login support, delayed delivery, coverage areas, and caller ID.
tldr.outcome: Gateways supporting SNPP have been deployed for nationwide paging and messaging. The protocol enables immediate feedback on delivery failures, unlike SMTP email, and provides precise control over message content.

facts.label: Level 1 commands
facts.value: PAGE, MESS, RESET, SEND, QUIT, HELP

today: RFC 1645 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1861. While some SNPP gateways were deployed for nationwide paging, the protocol has not achieved widespread adoption, with email-based paging gateways ultimately prevailing for most use cases.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
The primary motivation for SNPP is eliminating the need for modems and phone lines to deliver alphanumeric pages to radio paging terminals. Traditional page delivery to distant cities or countries requires complex coordination with paging carriers using convoluted protocols.

SNPP provides a standard protocol whereby pages can be delivered to individual paging terminals through the Internet. A key advantage is immediate notification of delivery problems. If a gateway is unreachable, the user discovers this immediately and can invoke an alternate plan, unlike SMTP email which may be deferred without notifying the sender.
sections.eli5: Instead of using a phone line and modem to send a page, you can send it through the Internet. When you send it, you immediately know if it worked or failed.

sections.title: Protocol Design and Philosophy
sections.content:
SNPP is sequence of commands and responses designed with simplicity in mind. The protocol works between a paging terminal and the Internet, acting as a direct shim between them. It intentionally leaves validation of paging information to the paging terminal itself.

SNPP uses numeric response codes organized in four categories: 2xx for successful continuation, 3xx to begin message input, 4xx for failures that terminate the connection, and 5xx for failures that allow the session to continue. This structure mirrors SMTP response codes, making the protocol familiar to Internet users.
sections.eli5: The protocol is simple on purpose. A client connects, tells the server who to page and what message to send, and the server immediately tells you if it worked or not.

sections.title: Level 1: Basic Commands
sections.content:
Level 1 commands provide a minimum implementation suitable for either TAP/IXO or TME protocols at the paging terminal. The PAGE command specifies the pager ID to receive the message. The MESS (Message) command provides a single-line message text. The SEND command finalizes the transaction and processes the page to the terminal.

The RESET command clears entered information, allowing users to correct mistakes during manual sessions. The QUIT command closes the session. An optional HELP command displays information about valid commands.

The transaction flow is straightforward: the client opens a connection, receives a 220 ready message, supplies the pager ID and message, issues SEND, receives confirmation, and sends QUIT.
sections.eli5: The basic steps are: tell the server which pager to reach (PAGE), what to say (MESS), send it (SEND), and quit. That's all you need to send a page.

sections.title: Level 2: Extended Capabilities
sections.content:
Level 2 adds features for more flexible paging scenarios. The DATA command, similar to SMTP's DATA, allows multiple-line messages instead of single-line text. The LOGIN command provides session authentication.

Optional enhancements enable pager-specific options per recipient: LEVEL specifies service level (Priority, Normal, delayed 5/15/30 minutes to 24 hours); COVERAGE selects alternate geographic regions; HOLDUNTIL requests delayed message delivery until a specified time; ALERT controls whether the pager alerts the user.

Message-oriented functions include SUBJECT for message subjects and CALLERID for caller identification. These extensions prepare SNPP for compatibility with the forthcoming TME (Telocator Message Entry) protocol standard.
sections.eli5: Advanced features let you send longer messages, log in, hold messages until a certain time, choose different delivery areas, and add a subject line. Different pagers in one session can get different settings.

sections.title: Why Not Use Email and SMTP?
sections.content:
While SMTP is reliable for most cases, it cannot guarantee delivery between all nodes at all times. Email messages are deferred when a gateway is down, leaving senders unaware of the delay. This creates problems for urgent pages: a message about a critical meeting that was supposed to start hours ago may arrive too late, after the meeting has ended.

SNPP provides absolute flexibility over message content. Email gateways must parse SMTP headers, eliminating the sender's control over formatting. For alphanumeric pagers with limited bandwidth, headers are wasteful. SNPP sends the message exactly as written, maximizing RF bandwidth utility.

The simplicity of SNPP also benefits manual users: telnet sessions to an SNPP gateway are far simpler than manually hacking a mail message into a gateway.
sections.eli5: Email doesn't tell you if it failed right away, and it adds lots of header information that wastes space on small pagers. SNPP tells you immediately if it worked and sends only what you write.
